meta.title: Social Engineering Incident Atlas India
meta.sampling_notice: The Atlas is purposively sampled and retrieval-driven. Case counts describe the reviewed corpus and must not be interpreted as national cybercrime prevalence or state rankings.
meta.attribution_notice: Actor records assess source-supported conduct and identity resolution. They are not findings of guilt.
meta.map_notice: Map markers show the state or UT coded for reviewed incidents. Marker location is an approximate state centroid, not an incident coordinate.
meta.citation: Hamzah. (2026). Social Engineering Incident Atlas India (v0.4.0). GitHub repository.

cases.case_title: Ramakrishna Mission Gwalior digital arrest fraud
cases.court_or_authority: High Court of Madhya Pradesh, Gwalior Bench
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Inspector / police official from Nashik Police
cases.reconnaissance_description: The caller used the complainant's name and claimed that a Canara Bank account had been opened using his Aadhaar details, but the public court record does not establish how those details were obtained.
cases.initial_contact_summary: On 17 March 2025 the Secretary of Ramakrishna Mission Ashram, Thatipur, Gwalior received a WhatsApp call from a person claiming to be an Inspector from Nashik Police.
cases.pretext_summary: The caller claimed that an FIR for money laundering had been registered, presented details of a purported Canara Bank account in the complainant's name with about INR 20 crore in transactions, sent a PDF bank statement via WhatsApp, and said the complainant had to cooperate with an investigation to avoid arrest.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Legitimacy theatre using police uniform, a police-office visual setting, purported official financial documents, secrecy instructions, and coercive compliance.
cases.requested_action: Cooperate with the purported investigation, disclose personal/family and Ashram financial information, remain available and isolated from outside verification, and transfer Ashram funds to accounts specified by the caller.
cases.victim_action: The complainant continued communicating, disclosed information, followed secrecy/isolation instructions, and transferred a total of INR 25,299,000 to multiple accounts between 17 March and 11 April 2025.
cases.other_evidence: Purported bank-statement PDF; memorandum statements; cheque/withdrawal records; mobile phone and SIM seizure; later court order recounts CDR relationships among several accused.
cases.attribution_target: Identified downstream accused network associated with communications and movement of funds; the original impersonating caller(s) remain unresolved in the public material reviewed.
cases.attribution_limitations: The public court material links several accused to beneficiary accounts, withdrawals, bank facilitation, devices, or communications with other accused, but does not conclusively identify the person who made the original WhatsApp impersonation call or prove that every downstream account holder knew the full social-engineering scheme.
cases.alternative_explanation: For some accused, the documented link may be limited to account provision, withdrawal, transaction facilitation, device/SIM association, or communication with co-accused rather than direct participation in the initial impersonation. Knowledge and intent remain matters for trial.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Direct digital attribution of the original WhatsApp caller(s), ideally through platform/provider records, device-level account artefacts, telecom correlation, and authenticated communication records tying the impersonation account to an operator.
cases.legal_provisions: BNS 61(2); BNS 111(3) (in some orders); BNS 238; BNS 319(2); BNS 318(4); BNS 308(2); BNS 336(2); BNS 337; BNS 338; BNS 336(3); BNS 340(2); Information Technology Act Section 66-D
cases.disposition: Trial remains pending in the public court material reviewed. Multiple accused have pursued bail or quashing applications. The latest direct order located for this coding pass, dated 6 May 2026, dismissed Ravi Kumar Sahani's second bail application.
cases.case_summary: According to repeated Madhya Pradesh High Court recitals of the prosecution case, the Secretary of Ramakrishna Mission Ashram in Gwalior was contacted on WhatsApp on 17 March 2025 by a person claiming to be a Nashik Police Inspector. The caller alleged that a money-laundering FIR concerned a Canara Bank account purportedly opened in the complainant's name, sent a PDF account statement, threatened arrest, and later used a video call showing a police-uniformed person in a police-office-like setting. The complainant was instructed not to disclose the interaction and was induced to provide financial information and transfer Ashram funds. Between 17 March and 11 April 2025, INR 25,299,000 was transferred to multiple accounts. Later court orders describe bank-account trails, withdrawals, seized phones/SIMs, and CDR links among several accused. The reviewed public material supports meaningful attribution to parts of the downstream transaction and communications network, but it does not conclusively identify the original impersonating caller.
cases.research_notes: Primary coding privileges repeated High Court recitals over early press reports where details conflict. An NDTV report states that funds went to 12 accounts and describes a 26-day episode; this supports known_account_count=12. Early press reporting contains some inconsistent details about the first contact and impersonated agency, so those details were not used where they conflicted with the judicial record. Pre-publication source audit completed 2026-08-16; structured coding rechecked against the registered public source(s). v0.2.0 full-corpus source-to-code re-audit completed 2026-09-04.

cases.case_title: VIP Profit Makers fake investment app fraud
cases.court_or_authority: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Person claiming to be Karan Subhash Arora, Assistant to Manager at MUNOTH CAPITAL LTD
cases.initial_contact_summary: In August 2025, the complainant received a WhatsApp call from a person claiming association with MUNOTH CAPITAL LTD and offering investment plans.
cases.pretext_summary: The caller claimed membership in a SEBI-listed investment company, added the complainant to a WhatsApp group named VIP PROFIT MAKERS with about 100 members, showed apparent examples of money doubling, and induced him to install an ALFA NAVIGATOR app and transfer funds to accounts supplied through the app.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Social proof through a large WhatsApp group and apparent examples of profitable investments; legitimacy borrowing from a claimed SEBI-listed company and an app-store link.
cases.requested_action: Join the investment group, install/register on ALFA NAVIGATOR, and transfer investment funds to designated bank accounts.
cases.victim_action: The complainant transferred multiple amounts to several bank accounts and later attempted to withdraw his funds.
cases.other_evidence: FIR reproduces the WhatsApp contact, app URL, named group, and detailed beneficiary bank accounts and transfer amounts.
cases.attribution_target: Petitioner Shivam Goyal and any operators of the WhatsApp group / app infrastructure.
cases.attribution_limitations: The bail order reproduces a detailed victim narrative but gives little detail explaining how the petitioner was technically or financially linked to the original inducement, beyond the fact that he was arrested and prosecuted in the FIR.
cases.alternative_explanation: The petitioner claimed that he had himself been duped by another person and was falsely implicated.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Specific digital or financial evidence connecting the petitioner to operation of the WhatsApp identity, ALFA NAVIGATOR infrastructure, or beneficiary accounts.
cases.disposition: Regular bail granted on 27 February 2026; trial pending and merits left open.
cases.case_summary: A Gurugram complainant was approached on WhatsApp by a purported representative of an investment company, added to a large group displaying apparent investment success, and induced to install a fake investment app. He transferred INR 8,248,021 to multiple bank accounts. When withdrawal was attempted, further money was demanded. The public bail order provides a rich social-engineering reconstruction but limited accused-specific attribution evidence.
cases.research_notes: Useful example of social proof and legitimacy engineering in fake-investment fraud. Known account count is seven distinct beneficiary accounts; the source lists nine transfers, with two account numbers reused. Pre-publication source audit completed 2026-08-16; structured coding rechecked against the registered public source(s). v0.2.0 full-corpus source-to-code re-audit completed 2026-09-04.

cases.case_title: Fake HR work-from-home task scam
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Woman calling herself Akansha, purported HR executive of Freelance Pvt. Ltd.
cases.initial_contact_summary: The complainant received a WhatsApp call from a woman presenting herself as an HR executive and offering paid work-from-home Google search/review tasks.
cases.pretext_summary: The caller promised payment for simple tasks, made small initial payments to build trust, then claimed free task coupons had expired and induced the complainant to pay for higher-income tasks.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Trust seeding through genuine small payouts before escalating to paid tasks; sunk-cost pressure when further payments were demanded to recover supposed earnings.
cases.requested_action: Perform online tasks, then make repeated payments for higher-return tasks and additional payments to unlock earnings.
cases.victim_action: The complainant made repeated deposits and lost INR 375,000.
cases.other_evidence: Calling numbers traced to waho.pro, hosted on a U.S.-based server; bank CCTV recorded cash withdrawal; WhatsApp chats recovered from a co-accused phone showed account details being shared.
cases.attribution_target: Aayush Goyal's alleged role in supplying/circulating mule bank accounts, distinct from the original HR impersonator.
cases.attribution_limitations: The complainant did not directly identify the applicant as the inducer. His alleged role arose through co-accused disclosures and WhatsApp chats showing bank-account sharing, rather than direct evidence that he made the original call.
cases.alternative_explanation: The applicant argued that his cryptocurrency-related activity was legitimate and that he neither received cheated money nor knew the complainant.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Direct linkage between the original HR impersonation account/calling infrastructure and identified human operators, plus full cryptocurrency transaction records tying mule-account circulation to fraudulent proceeds.
cases.disposition: Anticipatory bail granted on 15 December 2025; investigation and trial-related proceedings remained ongoing.
cases.case_summary: A Delhi complainant was approached through WhatsApp by a fake HR executive offering paid Google review tasks. Small initial payouts established trust, after which the victim was induced to pay for higher-value tasks and to make additional deposits when attempting to recover earnings, losing INR 375,000. Investigation traced funds through mule accounts, CCTV-recorded withdrawals and WhatsApp account-sharing chats, illustrating a multi-layered separation between social-engineering operators and financial infrastructure.
cases.research_notes: The source reports the calling infrastructure as waho.pro on a U.S.-based server, supporting a cross-border infrastructure dimension even though the victim and investigated network were in India. Pre-publication source audit completed 2026-08-16; structured coding rechecked against the registered public source(s). v0.2.0 full-corpus source-to-code re-audit completed 2026-09-04.

cases.case_title: Canada relative and medical emergency impersonation fraud
cases.court_or_authority: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Relative Satpal said to be living in Canada; second caller posed as bank official; third caller posed as Harjeet Singh.
cases.reconnaissance_description: The impersonator used the name of a real Canada-based relative and the victim's bank-account details in the pretext, but the public source does not establish whether this resulted from prior reconnaissance, leaked data, or another route.
cases.initial_contact_summary: The complainant received a WhatsApp call from a person claiming to be his Canada-based relative Satpal.
cases.pretext_summary: The impersonator claimed he would send INR 16.15 lakh to the complainant before returning to India, sent a fake transfer receipt, and a separate caller posed as an Axis Bank head-office employee to corroborate the transfer. The fake relative then requested urgent funds for a purported associate's hospitalized wife.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Layered corroboration using an apparent bank official; emotional pressure through a crying caller and medical emergency; exploitation of kinship and reciprocity after a fake incoming transfer.
cases.requested_action: Provide bank details/blank cheque image and urgently transfer INR 400,000, followed by a request for an additional INR 200,000.
cases.victim_action: The complainant sent a blank cheque image and transferred INR 400,000 before challenging the impersonator with family-verification questions.
cases.other_evidence: Fake INR 16.15 lakh transfer receipt sent on WhatsApp; beneficiary account belonged to petitioner's mother and had petitioner's mobile number registered.
cases.attribution_target: Petitioner Ratan Lal's alleged downstream role connected to the beneficiary account and registered mobile number.
cases.attribution_limitations: The order does not establish that the petitioner made the relative, bank-official, or medical-emergency calls. The bank account was in his mother's name and the petitioner disputed inducement.
cases.alternative_explanation: The petitioner may have been associated with the beneficiary account without being the social-engineering caller; knowledge and commission allegations remained prosecution claims.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Direct linkage of the impersonating WhatsApp/phone numbers to the human operators and authenticated device/platform records showing coordination with the beneficiary account.
cases.legal_provisions: BNS 318(4); BNS 319; BNS 336(3); BNS 338; BNS 340; BNS 61(B) as reported in source
cases.disposition: Regular bail granted on 21 January 2026; trial ongoing.
cases.case_summary: A Haryana victim was contacted on WhatsApp by a person impersonating a real relative living in Canada. The scheme used a forged transfer receipt and a second caller posing as an Axis Bank official to make the fake INR 16.15 lakh incoming transfer appear genuine. The relative then invoked a medical emergency and a crying third caller to induce an urgent INR 400,000 transfer. The victim detected the fraud by asking personal family questions the impersonator could not answer.
cases.research_notes: This case is especially valuable for studying layered corroboration, emotional urgency, and family-knowledge verification as a defensive social-engineering countermeasure. Pre-publication source audit completed 2026-08-16; structured coding rechecked against the registered public source(s). v0.2.0 full-corpus source-to-code re-audit completed 2026-09-04.

cases.case_title: Fake Yahoo customer care APK fraud against senior citizen
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Purported customer-care service for Yahoo email issue
cases.initial_contact_summary: A senior citizen searching online for help with a Yahoo email problem contacted a purported customer-care number found through an online search.
cases.pretext_summary: The purported support operator induced the complainant to download an APK and persuaded him to provide debit-card details while ostensibly resolving the email problem.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Search-result trust transfer: the victim treated a number surfaced through online search as legitimate customer support.
cases.requested_action: Download an APK and provide debit-card information.
cases.victim_action: The complainant downloaded the APK and disclosed debit-card details; about INR 14 lakh was initially siphoned and linked fixed deposits were later accessed/liquidated, raising the reported total loss to about INR 26 lakh.
cases.other_evidence: KYC/account-opening documents, transaction statements, CDRs, IPDRs, IMEI data, location charts, ATM CCTV and NCRP-linked account information.
cases.attribution_target: Sahil Khan's alleged cash-out / beneficiary role within an inter-State fraud network, separate from the fake customer-care operator.
cases.attribution_limitations: The public order strongly links the applicant to cash withdrawals, location data and receipt of funds but does not establish that he operated the fake customer-care number or APK.
cases.alternative_explanation: The applicant denied any role and argued that location coincidence was insufficient; original social-engineering and malware operators remain distinct from downstream cash-out actors.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Direct forensic attribution of the fake customer-care number/APK infrastructure and proof linking that operator layer to the downstream financial network.
cases.disposition: Anticipatory bail denied on 14 January 2026; investigation continuing.
cases.case_summary: A Delhi senior citizen searching online for Yahoo support contacted a fraudulent customer-care number, downloaded an APK and disclosed card information. The reported loss eventually reached about INR 26 lakh after linked fixed deposits were accessed. Investigation used bank KYC and transactions, CDR/IPDR/IMEI/location data and ATM CCTV to map an inter-State mule and cash-out network. The case illustrates the evidentiary separation between the social-engineering entry point and downstream financial actors.
cases.research_notes: One of the strongest cases in the pilot for combining human manipulation, malicious software installation and layered digital/physical attribution evidence. Pre-publication source audit completed 2026-08-16; structured coding rechecked against the registered public source(s). v0.2.0 full-corpus source-to-code re-audit completed 2026-09-04.

cases.case_title: Tekku Samurai cross-border tech-support fraud
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Microsoft or Apple representatives
cases.reconnaissance_description: Call-centre devices contained lists of Japanese telephone numbers and scripts/quotations, indicating systematic targeting of Japanese victims.
cases.initial_contact_summary: Victims encountered fake virus alerts/phishing prompts on malicious URLs and were instructed to call a displayed number.
cases.pretext_summary: Callers impersonating Microsoft or Apple claimed the victim's computer had technical problems, induced installation of remote-access software or purchase of antivirus/service packages, and obtained access to sensitive financial information.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Panic induction through fake virus alerts and brand impersonation, followed by scripted technical authority and remote-assistance framing.
cases.requested_action: Call the displayed number, install remote-access software or purchase purported technical services, and provide/payment-sensitive information.
cases.victim_action: Victims installed remote-access software and/or paid through gift cards or other channels; four Japanese victims were specifically identified in the FIR.
cases.remote_access_tool: Remote-access software; seized systems also showed Zoiper VoIP use
cases.other_evidence: SSDs, call logs, Japanese phone-number lists, fake Microsoft identity cards, victim banking screenshots, gift-card screenshots/codes, pitching scripts and quotations, partnership/rent/KYC records and bank profit transfers.
cases.attribution_target: Tekku Samurai call-centre operation and Komal Kumar's alleged ownership/management role.
cases.attribution_limitations: The order concerns bail and does not finally adjudicate guilt. It does not establish that the applicant personally made each victim call; the strength code concerns ownership/operational linkage to the documented call-centre system.
cases.alternative_explanation: The applicant argued he was merely an owner and that financial transfers from Bidder Media were legitimate commercial transactions unrelated to victim fraud.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Victim-specific linkage between particular call-centre agents/sessions and each fraudulent loss, plus complete foreign payment and remote-access logs.

cases.case_title: SMS-service closure phishing and vishing bank fraud
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Unknown caller claiming the victim needed to click a link to keep SMS service operational
cases.initial_contact_summary: The victim received an SMS containing a link followed by a phone call from an unknown person.
cases.pretext_summary: The caller said the victim had to click the link or his SMS service would be closed. After he clicked, unauthorised internet-banking transactions were made.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Service-interruption threat used to induce a security-sensitive action.
cases.requested_action: Click the SMS link to keep mobile/SMS service active.
cases.victim_action: The victim clicked the link; INR 260,000 was then transferred through two internet-banking transactions. He immediately reported the unauthorised transactions.
cases.other_evidence: Internet-banking login timestamps, OTP delivery records, beneficiary details, merchant code, RRN and IP address were examined in banking/ombudsman proceedings.
cases.attribution_target: Unknown attacker and mechanism by which banking credentials/OTPs were compromised.
cases.attribution_limitations: The litigation established the victim interacted with a suspicious link and that valid internet-banking authentication was used, but the exact technical compromise mechanism and attacker identity were not forensically established.
cases.alternative_explanation: The victim maintained he never shared OTPs and that malware or compromise transmitted credentials; the bank argued that clicking the suspicious link constituted customer negligence and enabled credential misuse.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Technical forensic examination of the device/link and attacker infrastructure sufficient to determine how credentials and OTPs were obtained and to identify the operator.
cases.legal_provisions: RBI Circular dated 06.07.2017 on customer liability for unauthorised electronic banking transactions
cases.disposition: Delhi High Court Division Bench allowed SBI's appeal on 29 May 2026 and set aside the earlier single-judge judgment; it stressed that unresolved technical questions required forensic examination rather than inference in writ proceedings.
cases.case_summary: An academician received an SMS link and a call warning that his SMS service would be closed unless he clicked. After doing so, two internet-banking transactions totalling INR 260,000 were executed. The victim denied sharing OTPs. The later appellate judgment is especially valuable for the Atlas because the court refused to infer the exact compromise mechanism without technical or forensic evidence, highlighting the gap between a documented social-engineering trigger and unresolved technical causation.
cases.research_notes: This is a civil/banking-liability case rather than a criminal prosecution, included because the underlying social-engineering incident and evidentiary uncertainty are richly documented. cases.case_title: Hacked superior WhatsApp payment impersonation
cases.case_number: FIR No.28/2025, Cyber Police Station West Delhi
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Reporting officer Pradeep Singh Kharola, CMD, India Trade Promotion Organisation
cases.reconnaissance_description: The fraud exploited a compromised WhatsApp account within an existing superior-subordinate communication context. The source does not establish a separate pre-contact reconnaissance process by the fraudster.
cases.initial_contact_summary: While the complainant was conversing with his reporting officer on WhatsApp, a request appeared asking him to transfer money to Rajan Kumar.
cases.pretext_summary: The message appeared to come from the complainant's reporting officer, first requesting INR 20,000 and then INR 25,000. A third request for INR 30,000 triggered verification, revealing that the officer's WhatsApp account had been hacked.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Exploitation of an existing organisational trust channel and superior authority; low-value escalation before a third request triggered verification.
cases.requested_action: Transfer INR 20,000, then INR 25,000, followed by a further INR 30,000 request.
cases.victim_action: The complainant transferred INR 45,000 through Paytm and Mobikwik before verifying the request.
cases.other_evidence: Jio Payment Bank and India Post Payment Bank accounts in applicant's name; CAF/CDR linked fraud mobile number to applicant; one account opened a day before the fraud and linked to three other cyber complaints.
cases.attribution_target: Rajan Kumar's alleged role as recipient/controller of payment accounts and mobile number connected to the impersonation fraud.
cases.attribution_limitations: The court stated that the petitioner allegedly hacked the superior's WhatsApp account, but the public order's strongest described evidence concerns accounts, mobile linkage, repeated complaints and use of funds rather than a detailed forensic account-takeover analysis.
cases.alternative_explanation: The applicant claimed a friend had taken his account details for receiving funds from abroad and denied the offence, although he returned the cheated amount.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Forensic/platform evidence showing how the superior's WhatsApp account was taken over and directly linking the takeover session/device to the accused.
cases.disposition: Anticipatory bail denied on 1 July 2025; investigation ongoing.
cases.case_summary: An employee received payment requests through the WhatsApp account of his reporting officer, a senior public-sector executive, and transferred INR 45,000 before a third request prompted verification. The officer's account had been hacked. Investigation linked the beneficiary accounts and a mobile number to the applicant, found that one account had been opened a day before the fraud, and identified similar complaints involving the same accounts. The case functions as a compact Indian analogue of executive-impersonation/BEC-style social engineering.
cases.research_notes: Useful bridge between account takeover and social engineering: the technical compromise created the trusted identity, while the fraud itself depended on organisational authority and contextual trust. Pre-publication source audit completed 2026-08-16; structured coding rechecked against the registered public source(s). v0.2.0 full-corpus source-to-code re-audit completed 2026-09-04.

cases.case_title: Airtel-to-CBI senior-citizen digital-arrest fraud
cases.case_number: FIR No.85/2025, P.S. Special Cell, Delhi
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Airtel officials, Mumbai Police and CBI officials
cases.initial_contact_summary: On 1 August 2025 a senior citizen in his late seventies received a landline call from people posing as Airtel officials.
cases.pretext_summary: The callers claimed his Aadhaar had been used to open a fraudulent Mumbai bank account, threatened telecom suspension, connected him to supposed Mumbai Police, shifted him to WhatsApp video, then claimed CBI involvement, a large bank fraud and terror funding while presenting an arrest warrant.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Telecom-service threat created the entry point; multiple government identities, terror-funding allegations and isolation sustained coercion.
cases.requested_action: Isolate, remain on video contact and make transfers to numerous accounts under the purported investigation.
cases.victim_action: The complainant made repeated transfers between 4 August and 4 September 2025 totalling INR 22.92 crore.
cases.other_evidence: Beneficiary-company records, linked mobile numbers, WhatsApp chats, alleged account/SIM procurement and same-day withdrawals.
cases.attribution_target: Applicants alleged to have supplied/controlled or operated beneficiary account infrastructure used to siphon funds.
cases.attribution_limitations: The public order develops evidence concerning account infrastructure and communications among downstream actors but does not establish that the applicants made the Airtel/Mumbai Police/CBI calls.
cases.alternative_explanation: Applicants disputed whether they were victims, peripheral account holders or active participants; the court treated those role questions as matters for continued investigation/trial.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Direct evidence linking the original caller identities and WhatsApp video accounts to identified operators.
cases.disposition: Four bail applications, including regular and anticipatory bail pleas, were dismissed on 22 April 2026.

cases.initial_contact_summary: On 7 December 2024 the complainant received a phone call from a person falsely representing himself as an RBI official.

cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Provider/device attribution for the digital-arrest WhatsApp numbers and direct evidence tying victim-facing identities to the downstream account network.
cases.disposition: Regular bail dismissed on 30 March 2026; observations expressly not to influence trial.

cases.initial_contact_summary: On 9 January 2024 the complainant encountered a social-media advertisement and link for an Indian Stock Investment Learning Group allegedly founded by BlackRock Capital.
cases.pretext_summary: After joining the El BlackRock Stocks Pull Up Group on WhatsApp and observing activity for about 15 days, the complainant was invited to open an institutional account in Angel One, upload identity details and invest; withdrawal later required a 30% commission paid separately.

cases.case_summary: A Delhi investor observed a BlackRock-branded WhatsApp investment group for around 15 days, then submitted identity details and invested INR 4.96 million through a purported Angel One institutional-account workflow. cases.initial_contact_summary: The complainant and family were drawn into WhatsApp communications with people impersonating multiple government and law-enforcement bodies.
cases.pretext_summary: The perpetrators used forged law-enforcement and financial-crime documents, purported PMLA/FEMA action and continuous WhatsApp video surveillance to claim the complainant was under investigation and digital arrest.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: The complainant, wife and daughter were kept under sustained digital surveillance; the scheme escalated to eliciting banking credentials and stock details.
cases.requested_action: Remain under video surveillance, disclose banking credentials and investment information, sell shares, and transfer funds under purported official control.
cases.victim_action: The family complied with surveillance and financial instructions; the complainant’s accounts/stocks were used to transfer or extort INR 2,30,70,620.

cases.attribution_limitations: The source itself notes no material showing the applicant made the WhatsApp calls, impersonated officers, sent forged documents or directly induced the complainant; his alleged role is downstream financial facilitation.
cases.alternative_explanation: Forwarding OTPs/account association may establish a financial facilitation role without proving participation in the initial social-engineering interaction; knowledge and intent remain trial issues.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Direct platform/device attribution of the victim-facing WhatsApp accounts and evidence linking those operators to the financial-facilitation layer.
cases.disposition: Regular bail after charge sheet dismissed on 14 July 2026; trial court directed to expedite trial.

cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Romantic suitor using employment and marriage assurances
cases.reconnaissance_description: The appellate court found that after Facebook contact the accused gathered information about the victim’s family background and personal circumstances and exploited her employment-related vulnerability.
cases.initial_contact_summary: The accused initiated contact through Facebook and persisted after the victim initially declined the friend request.
cases.pretext_summary: He offered help securing employment while presenting himself as a genuine romantic suitor intending marriage, shifted communication to WhatsApp, and later used clandestinely recorded intimate material for coercion and threats of social-media publication.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Persistent contact, employment assistance, marriage assurance, migration to private messaging and intimate-material threats created progressive emotional control.
cases.requested_action: Maintain private communication/relationship and comply with demands under threats that intimate material would be circulated.
cases.victim_action: The victim accepted communication after repeated persuasion and later complied under coercion; no focal monetary loss is normalized.
cases.other_evidence: Seized Apple MacBook and other devices, FSL cloning/extraction, expert reports, victim identification of recovered material and judicial discussion of authenticity/tampering/Section 65B.
cases.attribution_target: Convicted appellant as the social-engineering and coercive actor.
cases.attribution_limitations: The judgment provides unusually strong adjudicated attribution, but the Atlas still limits the record to what this judgment establishes and avoids republishing sensitive source material.
cases.alternative_explanation: The defence challenged consent, device/evidence chain, possible manipulation and Section 65B issues; the appellate court rejected these arguments after detailed evidentiary analysis.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: No major attribution gap remains at the level of the convicted appellant; platform-side records could add source redundancy but are not necessary to the final judicial finding.
cases.legal_provisions: IPC 376(2)(n), 417, 354A, 294(b), 354C; IT Act 66E and other charged provisions as discussed in judgment
cases.disposition: Criminal appeal dismissed on 14 July 2026; trial-court conviction and sentence dated 14 June 2023 confirmed.
cases.case_summary: A Madras High Court appellate judgment describes a social-engineering sequence beginning with persistent Facebook contact, false employment and marriage assurances, migration to private WhatsApp communication, and later coercion using clandestinely recorded intimate material. Unlike most Atlas cases, attribution is supported by a final conviction plus extensive seized-device and forensic evidence whose authenticity and preservation were expressly litigated and upheld.
cases.research_notes: Sensitive sexual details and unnecessary identifiers are deliberately omitted. This case is included for its exceptionally rich electronic-evidence authentication analysis and final adjudicatory posture. Second-pass source, coding, procedural-posture and privacy audit completed 2026-08-26. v0.2.0 full-corpus source-to-code re-audit completed 2026-09-04.

cases.case_title: Matrimonial relationship with alleged Army-officer impersonation
cases.case_number: Cr.MP(M) No.607/2025; FIR No.20/2025, P.S. Manali
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Alleged former/currently associated Indian Army officer with special-mission claims
cases.reconnaissance_description: The parties were introduced through a matrimonial context and the applicant allegedly supplied detailed personal/property/professional representations and Army-uniform media to build trust.
cases.initial_contact_summary: The complainant, who had created a matrimonial profile, was introduced to the applicant as a divorced man looking to remarry and was contacted on 1 October 2024.
cases.pretext_summary: The complainant alleged the applicant represented himself as an Army officer/former officer on special assignments, shared photographs/videos in uniform, made property/business claims and expressed a desire to marry, then repeatedly requested money for hotel/business needs.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Military prestige, marriage intent, asserted assets and personal vulnerability formed the trust structure; later allegations included pressure/blackmail.
cases.requested_action: Provide money for alleged business/financial needs and continue the relationship on the stated marriage premise.
cases.victim_action: The complaint alleged INR 8.15 lakh provided in cash and electronic payments; police status reports later described INR 4.15 lakh through Google Pay/cheque and return of that amount.
cases.other_evidence: Mobile sent to RFSL; service-provider subscriber information; missing hotel CCTV because backup retained only 15 days; Army dress sought for recovery.
cases.attribution_target: Applicant’s alleged personal identity representations and relationship conduct.
cases.attribution_limitations: The public source contains a material conflict between the complaint’s INR 8.15 lakh figure and the police status report’s INR 4.15 lakh electronic transfer figure, while core deception/relationship issues were explicitly left for trial.
cases.alternative_explanation: The applicant characterized the matter as a civil/relationship dispute, said money had been repaid and disputed criminal intent; the court made anticipatory-bail protection absolute.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Completed RFSL/device analysis and independent evidence resolving the claimed Army identity/professional representations and the disputed financial chronology.
cases.legal_provisions: BNS 69, 204, 318(4); zero FIR also referenced BNS 316(2), 318(4), 61, 64(2)(m)
cases.disposition: Interim anticipatory-bail protection made absolute on 25 July 2025 after the applicant joined investigation and charge sheet was filed.
cases.case_summary: A matrimonially introduced relationship involved allegations that the applicant falsely presented himself as an Army officer, used uniform photographs/videos and marriage intentions to build trust, and repeatedly sought money. The source is analytically useful precisely because the financial figures conflict between the complaint and police status reports and the court left key relationship/deception questions for trial. The Atlas therefore does not normalize a single loss amount or overstate attribution.
cases.research_notes: financial_loss_inr intentionally blank because complaint states INR 815,000 while police status report states INR 415,000 through Google Pay/cheque and says it was returned. The conflict is preserved rather than reconciled by researcher inference. cases.case_title: OLX payment and UPI manipulation fraud
cases.court_or_authority: State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, U.T. Chandigarh
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Purported OLX counterparty expected to send INR 8,000
cases.initial_contact_summary: The complainant expected an INR 8,000 payment from an individual who contacted him through OLX.
cases.pretext_summary: The OLX counterparty asked for UPI details or a scan-code interaction to facilitate receipt of payment, moved the interaction to WhatsApp, and sent a nominal INR 5 credit before unauthorized debits followed.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: A small INR 5 credit functioned as a trust/verification signal immediately before larger unauthorized debits.
cases.requested_action: Share UPI information/perform the requested scan-code interaction to receive an expected marketplace payment.
cases.victim_action: The complainant performed the requested UPI interaction and then saw four debits of INR 8,000, INR 8,000, INR 24,000 and INR 24,000.
cases.attribution_target: Unknown OLX/WhatsApp counterparty; the adjudication focused on bank liability rather than offender identity.
cases.attribution_limitations: The Commission did not identify or attribute the social-engineering interaction to a named offender; its decision concerned whether the disputed transactions were unauthorized and the bank’s customer-liability obligations.
cases.alternative_explanation: The bank argued customer negligence/authorization; the Commission found the complainant had not shared OTP or bank account details and had reported promptly.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Offender-side platform, UPI beneficiary, device and account records sufficient to identify/control-attribution the OLX/WhatsApp counterparty.
cases.legal_provisions: Consumer-protection/banking liability context; RBI circular dated 06.07.2017 discussed in decision
cases.disposition: State Consumer Commission dismissed SBI’s appeal on 30 September 2024 and upheld refund of INR 64,000 with interest.
cases.case_summary: An OLX counterparty asked a Chandigarh complainant to share UPI details or scan a code so an expected INR 8,000 payment could be received. A nominal INR 5 credit was followed by four unauthorized debits totalling INR 64,000. The appellate consumer decision is valuable for reconstructing the manipulation and banking evidence, but it contains no offender attribution, so attribution is marked not assessed.
cases.research_notes: Included to broaden source stage and demonstrate that relevant social-engineering reconstruction can arise in civil/consumer adjudication, not only criminal bail orders. Audit correction: the focal manipulation is coded as marketplace_fraud without a secondary phishing label because the adjudicatory record does not establish credential harvesting, a deceptive login page, or OTP/PIN disclosure. Second-pass source, coding, procedural-posture and privacy audit completed 2026-08-26. v0.2.0 full-corpus source-to-code re-audit completed 2026-09-04.

cases.case_title: Microsoft and Amazon tech-support remote-access fraud network
cases.court_or_authority: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Microsoft and Amazon support identities; purported Federal Reserve safety accounts
cases.initial_contact_summary: Foreign victims were exposed to fake pop-up alerts purporting to be from Microsoft and prompted to call VoIP-based support numbers.
cases.pretext_summary: Call-centre operators allegedly posed as Microsoft/Amazon support staff, persuaded victims to install TeamViewer or AnyDesk, falsely claimed computers and identities were compromised, and told victims to move funds to accounts purportedly managed by the Federal Reserve for protection.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Technical-support authority and fabricated account-compromise risk converted remote access into financial coercion.
cases.requested_action: Call the support number, install remote-access software, grant computer access and transfer funds to purported protective Federal Reserve accounts.
cases.victim_action: Multiple U.S. victims allegedly granted remote access and transferred funds; the network was alleged to have defrauded victims of about US$15 million overall.
cases.other_evidence: Call-centre search material, IPDR/FBI corroboration, financial/shell-entity trail, Hong Kong accounts, cryptocurrency and hawala allegations.
cases.attribution_target: Applicant’s alleged leadership/beneficiary role in the organized call-centre and money-laundering network.
cases.attribution_limitations: The source is an anticipatory-bail/PMLA proceeding and describes allegations against a network; the Atlas does not treat those allegations as final findings of the applicant’s exact operational role.
cases.alternative_explanation: Applicant contested ED allegations and sought pre-arrest protection; procedural findings about abscondence/proclamation do not substitute for final adjudication of the substantive fraud allegations.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Final trial-stage findings tying specific victim-facing calls, remote sessions and financial movements to identified operators/roles across the network.
cases.legal_provisions: PMLA 2002; underlying CBI FIR references IPC 120B, 420, 467, 468, 471 and IT Act 66D
cases.disposition: Anticipatory-bail petition dismissed on 17 August 2026; the applicant had been declared a proclaimed person in the underlying proceedings.
cases.case_summary: An alleged Delhi/NCR tech-support network targeted U.S. victims with Microsoft/Amazon-branded pop-ups, VoIP support calls and remote-access tools such as TeamViewer and AnyDesk. Victims were told their systems and identities were compromised and were induced to move money to supposed Federal Reserve accounts. The order alleges about US$15 million in losses and a layered international laundering path, while applicant-specific guilt remains unadjudicated at this stage.
cases.research_notes: financial_loss_inr intentionally blank because the source states losses in U.S. dollars and the Atlas does not convert currency using researcher-selected exchange rates. Cross-border dimension coded yes. Audit correction: the order reports FBI/IP data, malware-related findings and seized digital records, but does not clearly report a formal forensic examination; the forensic-examination field is therefore not_reported. Second-pass source, coding, procedural-posture and privacy audit completed 2026-08-26. v0.2.0 full-corpus source-to-code re-audit completed 2026-09-04.

cases.case_title: Canada-relative and escalating emergency family impersonation fraud
cases.court_or_authority: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
cases.case_number: FIR No.26/2023, Police Station Cyber Crime Hansi
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Purported father-in-law of the complainant’s Canada-based niece and associated relatives
cases.reconnaissance_description: The caller knew that the complainant had a niece in Canada and used that real family connection, but the public order does not establish how the information was obtained.
cases.initial_contact_summary: On 6 November 2023 the complainant received a phone call from a person claiming to be the father-in-law of his niece who lived in Canada.
cases.pretext_summary: The caller first claimed to be sending INR 10 lakh and supplied a false transaction image, then introduced repeated medical-emergency, death/body-release, debt-repayment and overseas-police-custody stories to obtain escalating transfers.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Kinship trust, sympathy, fabricated proof of an incoming transfer, repeated crisis escalation and persistent calling every few minutes.
cases.requested_action: Transfer money to bank accounts, UPI identifiers and wallet destinations supplied by the callers to meet successive purported family emergencies.
cases.victim_action: The complainant made repeated bank, UPI and wallet transfers over several weeks, reporting a total loss of INR 3,037,699.
cases.other_evidence: The bail order records recovery of mobile phones, SIM cards and ATM cards from the petitioner and a co-accused disclosure naming him.
cases.attribution_target: Petitioner’s alleged downstream role in the family-impersonation fraud network, distinct from the unidentified caller persona.
cases.attribution_limitations: Recovered phones/SIMs/ATM cards and a co-accused disclosure associate the petitioner with the investigation but the order does not establish that he operated the family persona or made the victim-facing calls.
cases.alternative_explanation: Possession of communication or payment artefacts can reflect a downstream or facilitation role rather than authorship of the original impersonation.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Telecom/platform and device artefacts tying the specific victim-facing numbers and WhatsApp accounts to identified human operators and to the receiving-account network.
cases.legal_provisions: IPC 406; IPC 420; IPC 467; IPC 468; IPC 471; IPC 120B
cases.disposition: Regular bail granted on 30 August 2024; merits reserved for trial.
cases.case_summary: A Haryana complainant was approached by a caller exploiting a real Canada-based family connection. A false incoming-transfer image and a sequence of medical, death, debt and overseas-custody emergencies induced repeated transfers totalling INR 3,037,699. The bail record links the petitioner to recovered phones, SIMs and ATM cards but does not identify him as the family-impersonation caller.
cases.research_notes: Included to strengthen family-impersonation coverage and to preserve the distinction between victim-facing identity fraud and downstream device/payment association. cases.case_title: Fake Paytm customer-care callback fraud
cases.case_number: W.P.(CRL.) 685/2023; FIR No.101/2022, Cyber Police Station South East Delhi
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Purported Paytm customer-care executive
cases.reconnaissance_description: The victim initiated contact after finding a purported Paytm support number through Google; no targeted pre-contact reconnaissance is reported.
cases.initial_contact_summary: The complainant searched Google for a Paytm customer-care number, called it, and after the call disconnected received a callback from another number.
cases.pretext_summary: The callback caller claimed to be a Paytm support executive and kept the complainant engaged in conversation while three unauthorized debits totalling INR 50,000 occurred.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Search-result trust transfer and immediate callback continuity made the caller appear connected to the support request.
cases.requested_action: Continue the purported customer-support interaction; the public order does not specify the exact technical action or credential requested.
cases.victim_action: The complainant engaged with the purported support caller; INR 50,000 was debited in three instalments.
cases.other_evidence: Paytm transaction information and IDFC Bank KYC records traced the cheated amount directly to a proprietorship account associated with the petitioner.
cases.attribution_target: Petitioner’s role as proprietor of the account that directly received the focal cheated amount, distinct from the unidentified Paytm-support caller.
cases.attribution_limitations: Direct receipt of the cheated amount in the petitioner’s business account does not establish that he made the support call, controlled the victim’s device, or knew the origin of every credit; investigation was incomplete.
cases.alternative_explanation: The petitioner asserted that the money reached his account without his knowledge and later returned it.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Telecom/device evidence identifying the fake support caller and technical evidence explaining the alleged mobile compromise and connecting that operator to the receiving account.
cases.disposition: Delhi High Court dismissed the petition to quash the FIR on 13 September 2023; investigation remained incomplete and no charge sheet had yet been filed.
cases.case_summary: A Delhi professional searching Google for Paytm support received a callback from a purported customer-care executive and lost INR 50,000 during the interaction. The money was traced to a proprietorship account associated with the quashing petitioner, but the public order does not establish that the account-linked person was the victim-facing caller.

cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Bank Manager

cases.case_title: WhatsApp managing-director impersonation and corporate payment diversion
cases.case_number: Anticipatory Bail Application No.1492/2025; Crime Register No.72/2025, Khopoli Police Station
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Managing Director of the employee’s company
cases.reconnaissance_description: The imposter targeted the company’s General Manager (Finance), adopted the Managing Director’s identity and exploited the company’s existing WhatsApp-based payment-approval workflow.
cases.initial_contact_summary: On 8 January 2025 an unknown WhatsApp user contacted the company’s General Manager (Finance), claimed to be the Managing Director and asked that a new number be saved.
cases.pretext_summary: Between 9 and 17 January the imposter sent payment instructions that appeared to continue the company’s established approval workflow. The employee also exchanged contemporaneous approval messages with the real Managing Director, which the High Court treated as supporting his claimed bona fide belief.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Executive authority, continuity with an established internal payment process and trusted-channel mimicry.
cases.requested_action: Process RTGS transfers to bank accounts furnished by the person impersonating the Managing Director.
cases.victim_action: The finance employee processed transfers totalling INR 55,000,000 to third-party accounts. About INR 13,100,000 was later recovered by freezing one account.
cases.other_evidence: The High Court considered the real Managing Director’s contemporaneous WhatsApp approvals, the destination-account investigation and recovery after an account freeze.
cases.attribution_target: Unknown Managing-Director impersonator, beneficiary-account network, and the prosecution’s alleged insider/facilitation theory concerning the finance employee.
cases.attribution_limitations: The attack itself is well reconstructed, but the imposter remains unidentified. The High Court found no material linking the finance employee to the imposter or destination accounts and said the contemporaneous messages supported his bona fide-belief explanation.
cases.alternative_explanation: The employee may have been a manipulated organisational insider rather than a colluding participant; the High Court found negligence or lack of diligence insufficient to establish criminal complicity at that stage.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Platform/device records identifying the imposter and end-to-end evidence linking the impersonating WhatsApp account to the controllers of the receiving accounts.
cases.disposition: Anticipatory bail allowed on 17 September 2025; the High Court found no material showing applicant-imposter nexus or personal gain, while the underlying fraud investigation/trial remained distinct.
cases.case_summary: A corporate finance employee received WhatsApp instructions from an unknown person impersonating the company’s Managing Director and processed INR 55 million in transfers. The record is valuable because the High Court separately examined whether the manipulated employee was himself complicit and found the available material supported his bona fide-belief explanation rather than deliberate collusion.
cases.research_notes: First Atlas case centered on executive-authority impersonation inside a live corporate payment workflow. Gross diverted amount is coded; later recovery of INR 13.1 million is preserved in narrative rather than silently netted. Second-pass source-to-code and privacy audit completed 2026-08-26. v0.2.0 full-corpus source-to-code re-audit completed 2026-09-04.

cases.initial_contact_summary: The complainant received an SMS stating that his KYC had been suspended and was then contacted by a person presenting himself as a KYC-support representative.

cases.case_title: Court-staff influence impersonation and electronic-evidence failure case
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Purported court employee/person with influence over judges, police and political actors
cases.reconnaissance_description: The messages referred to the complainant’s pending property litigation and promised influence over a favourable court order, showing case-specific knowledge even though its source was not established.
cases.initial_contact_summary: The complainant received repeated messages/calls and a letter from a person presenting himself as a court-connected operator who could influence a pending property case.
cases.pretext_summary: The sender demanded INR 15–20 lakh in exchange for securing a favourable court outcome and threatened death if the demand was not met. The prosecution later attempted to connect the communications to accused persons through SIM/CAF/CDR and related electronic material.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Claimed privileged access to judicial/police systems coupled with violent threats.
cases.requested_action: Pay INR 15–20 lakh in return for a favourable court order and to avoid threatened harm.
cases.victim_action: The public judgment describes repeated demands and threats but does not establish delivery of the demanded property; the court treated the extortion case as unproved.
cases.other_evidence: The prosecution relied on CAF/KYC, CDR and other secondary electronic records, but the court identified conflicting SIM-registration evidence, missing witnesses and invalid Section 65-B certification.
cases.attribution_target: Accused persons alleged to have operated the court-connected persona and threatening communications.
cases.attribution_limitations: The final court found the prosecution failed to prove the accused sent the messages or committed the charged offences. SIM-registration evidence conflicted and electronic records were held inadmissible for want of valid Section 65-B certification.
cases.alternative_explanation: The unknown “court staff” persona may not have been operated by the accused persons charged; subscriber/CAF association did not resolve actual use of the critical number.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Admissible, authenticated telecom/electronic records and reliable subscriber/device evidence connecting the critical communications to the accused human operators.
cases.legal_provisions: IPC 419; IPC 420; IPC 386; IPC 506; IPC 201; IPC 511; IPC 34; IT Act 66A (as charged/recorded)
cases.disposition: All accused acquitted by final judgment dated 27 February 2026.
cases.case_summary: A Bengaluru complainant facing a property dispute received messages from a purported court-connected person demanding INR 15–20 lakh for a favourable order and threatening death. The case is a useful negative example of association failing to mature into admissible attribution.

cases.case_title: Facebook relationship manipulation and false-suicide sextortion scheme
cases.case_number: CRMP No.1371/2026; Crime No.11/2024, Cyber Range Bilaspur
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Online female social/relationship persona and later purported friends/associates
cases.reconnaissance_description: The complainant shared family problems during sustained WhatsApp communications; the subsequent pressure exploited that disclosed emotional context.
cases.initial_contact_summary: The complainant accepted a Facebook friend request and began WhatsApp calls/chats with the online persona, sharing details of family problems.
cases.pretext_summary: The persona described abandonment/harassment by her family and induced transfers using a QR code. After an in-person meeting, callers claiming to be her friends/associates threatened to implicate the complainant in a false suicide/police case and to circulate obscene photographs/videos unless further payments were made.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Relationship-building, emotional disclosure, sympathy, shame/reputational threat and fear of false criminal implication.
cases.requested_action: Transfer money online and in cash, and continue paying under threats of a false suicide/police case and publication of intimate/obscene material.
cases.victim_action: The complainant alleged online transfers of INR 729,199 and cash payments of INR 1,300,000, totalling INR 2,029,199.
cases.other_evidence: The prosecution narrative refers to Facebook/WhatsApp communications, QR-code transfers, handwritten notes, obscene photographs/videos and later charge-sheet proceedings.
cases.attribution_target: Petitioners’ alleged participation in the relationship/extortion scheme, distinct from the unresolved operator identity of each online persona and threatening call.
cases.attribution_limitations: The High Court’s 2026 judgment quashed proceedings on the basis of compromise, not a merits determination of which petitioner operated each persona, call or payment channel. The source does not reproduce a detailed actor-specific digital attribution chain.
cases.alternative_explanation: Settlement/quashing does not establish innocence or guilt, and the existence of a charged petitioner does not by itself identify the original Facebook/WhatsApp operator.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Platform, device, telecom and payment records mapping the social persona, threatening callers and financial recipients to individual actors.
cases.legal_provisions: BNS 318(4); BNS 308(2); BNS 238; BNS 3(5); IT Act 66D
cases.disposition: On 14 May 2026 the Chhattisgarh High Court quashed the remaining criminal proceedings after an amicable settlement; the order did not adjudicate the underlying allegations on merits.
cases.case_summary: A Facebook friendship developed into sustained WhatsApp communication and emotional disclosure. The complainant alleged that sympathy-based transfers were followed by threats of a false suicide case, police complaint and circulation of obscene material, leading to total payments of about INR 2.03 million. The later High Court closure was compromise-based rather than an attribution finding.
cases.research_notes: Included because it has a clear focal victim and attack sequence, unlike network-only records screened out during the same batch. Second-pass source-to-code and privacy audit completed 2026-08-26. v0.2.0 full-corpus source-to-code re-audit completed 2026-09-04.

cases.case_title: FedEx narcotics pretext and Mumbai Cyber Crime digital-arrest fraud
cases.case_number: Bail Application No.1074/2026; Crime No.24/2023, Cyber Crime Police Station Palakkad
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: FedEx courier personnel and Mumbai Cyber Crime police
cases.initial_contact_summary: The complainant was called and told that a FedEx parcel purportedly sent by her to Taiwan contained narcotic drugs.
cases.pretext_summary: The callers escalated the courier story into a criminal-prosecution threat, presented themselves as Mumbai Cyber Crime police and said the complainant had to pay money to save herself from prosecution.

cases.attribution_target: Applicant’s alleged account-control/routing role and other accused persons’ cash-out/financial roles, distinct from the original FedEx/police callers.

cases.alternative_explanation: A bank-account routing role can be narrower than operation of the victim-facing digital-arrest pretext.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Telecom/device evidence identifying the original FedEx and police impersonators and linking those callers to the financial-routing network.
cases.legal_provisions: IPC 419; IPC 420; IT Act 66C; IT Act 66D
cases.disposition: Pre-arrest bail dismissed on 19 March 2026; the Kerala High Court held the investigation was at a preliminary stage and custodial interrogation was necessary.

cases.case_title: Spoofed CBI and MHA official impersonation extortion conspiracy
cases.case_number: Criminal Revision Case No.199/2025; C.C.No.6061/2024; CBI RC 01(A)/2020
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Senior Government of India officials associated with CBI/MHA and related official influence
cases.reconnaissance_description: The alleged scheme targeted persons facing investigations and used case-specific promises of favourable intervention, official identities/numbers and intermediary relationships.
cases.initial_contact_summary: The prosecution alleged a conspiracy in which spoofed official government numbers and intermediaries were used to approach persons facing investigations.
cases.pretext_summary: The actors allegedly impersonated or invoked senior Government of India/CBI/MHA authority, promised favourable settlement of investigative matters and demanded enormous payments, including a source-described INR 100 crore demand in one instance.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Official-number spoofing, claimed access to senior government authority and exploitation of targets’ fear of ongoing investigations.
cases.requested_action: Pay large sums in return for purported influence over or favourable resolution of investigative/criminal matters.
cases.victim_action: The reviewed revision order describes demands and attempted extortion; it does not establish a completed focal transfer suitable for coding as financial loss.
cases.other_evidence: The prosecution material described WhatsApp chats, telephonic surveillance, spoofed calls from official government numbers, witness statements and alleged coordination among accused persons.
cases.attribution_target: Petitioner’s alleged coordinator/conspiracy role in an extortion-by-impersonation network.
cases.attribution_limitations: The High Court was reviewing a discharge/revision question, not deciding guilt. It found sufficient material to proceed but expressly left proof of the charges to trial.
cases.alternative_explanation: The petitioner argued that he was himself a victim/was excluded from the core conspiracy and that the prosecution material did not conclusively establish his involvement.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Trial-tested evidence connecting each spoofed call, government persona and extortion demand to specific human operators and establishing the petitioner’s knowledge/intent beyond the charge-stage threshold.
cases.legal_provisions: IPC 120B; IPC 419; IPC 420; IPC 384 and related conspiracy/extortion provisions as recorded in underlying proceedings
cases.disposition: Telangana High Court dismissed the criminal revision on 2 March 2026, holding there was sufficient material for the petitioner to face trial and that a mini-trial was impermissible at the discharge stage.
cases.case_summary: A CBI-investigated conspiracy allegedly used spoofed official government numbers and claimed access to senior CBI/MHA officials to demand huge payments from persons facing investigations in return for favourable outcomes. The case expands the Atlas into official-influence extortion and is useful for separating charge-stage evidentiary sufficiency from final attribution.
cases.research_notes: No financial_loss_inr is coded because the reviewed order describes demands, including INR 100 crore, but does not establish a completed focal payment. Second-pass source-to-code and privacy audit completed 2026-08-26. v0.2.0 full-corpus source-to-code re-audit completed 2026-09-04.

cases.requested_action: Visit the linked HDFC-looking page and enter net-banking credentials.
cases.victim_action: The complainant followed the link and entered his customer ID and I-Pin; unauthorized beneficiaries were later added and INR 223,960 was transferred.
cases.other_evidence: CERT-In phishing-infrastructure analysis; Section 65-B certificates; account-opening forms; ATM/debit card and cheque evidence; three mobile phones and two SIM cards sent to GEQD Hyderabad.
cases.attribution_target: Freeman Anosike Aluma's alleged coordination/receipt role and the unresolved phishing operator(s).
cases.attribution_limitations: The trial conviction was set aside because a potentially vital GEQD expert report on three phones and two SIM cards had not been placed before the trial court. The public appellate record does not establish that the appellant personally sent the phishing email or operated the phishing website.
cases.alternative_explanation: The appellant denied involvement and argued that actual beneficiaries had been treated as witnesses; the missing expert report could materially affect the technical linkage.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: The GEQD expert report and device-level evidence capable of connecting a specific human to the phishing infrastructure and relevant communications.
cases.legal_provisions: IPC Section 379; IPC Section 120-B; Information Technology Act Section 66
cases.disposition: Trial conviction and sentence were set aside on 16 October 2018 and the matter was remanded for fresh appreciation after obtaining/considering the GEQD expert report.
cases.case_summary: A bank customer received a fake HDFC software-upgrade email, followed a link and disclosed net-banking credentials. Three beneficiaries were added and INR 223,960 was transferred. The investigation produced bank records, subscriber forms, CDRs, login/IP evidence, Section 65-B certificates and CERT-In analysis showing infrastructure routed through multiple countries. Witness evidence linked the appellant to arrangement and receipt of cash from a beneficiary account. However, three mobile phones and two SIM cards had been sent for GEQD examination and the resulting expert report was never placed before the trial court. The appellate court treated that omission as sufficiently important to set aside the conviction and remand the case. The record therefore combines a rich phishing reconstruction with a major evidentiary gap at the human-attribution layer.
cases.research_notes: Wave 1A corrective expansion. Exact incident dates are supported by the appellate record. Cross-border coding reflects documented US/France/Germany/Canada infrastructure, not a finding about offender nationality. Conviction status is not_yet_adjudicated because the trial conviction was set aside and the case remanded.

actors.alternative_explanation: He denied involvement and argued the actual beneficiaries were witnesses rather than accused.
actors.relationship_note: Human identity is resolved, but conduct attribution remains non-final after remand.

cases.case_title: Hacked-email impersonation and NRE transfer fraud
cases.case_number: First Appeal No.52 of 2016; CC No.21/2013
cases.platform_primary: Email / Canara Bank NRE transfer workflow
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: NRE account holder Vijayakumaran Raghavan
cases.reconnaissance_description: Unknown operators had access to or imitated the complainant's email identity and used transaction-style instructions and scanned signed requests in the banking workflow.
cases.initial_contact_summary: After the account holder's registered email had been compromised, fraudulent email instructions were sent to the Canara Bank branch handling his NRE accounts.
cases.pretext_summary: Unknown operators represented themselves as the account holder and issued apparently routine transfer instructions, relying on the compromised/imitated email identity and transaction documents.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Business-process familiarity and identity continuity were used to make fraudulent transfer instructions appear routine.
cases.requested_action: Process transfer instructions represented as coming from the NRE account holder.
cases.victim_action: Bank personnel processed disputed instructions, closing fixed-deposit funds and transferring a total of USD 86,500 abroad.
cases.other_evidence: Bank statements, disputed email instructions, scanned signed requests, FIR and consumer-forum evidence.
cases.attribution_target: Unknown operator(s) of the compromised/spoofed email instructions and overseas transfer endpoints.
cases.attribution_limitations: The consumer proceedings establish the disputed transfers and bank-handling failures but do not identify the human operator who compromised or imitated the email account or controlled the overseas receiving endpoints.
cases.alternative_explanation: The bank argued that the account holder had not properly replaced the registered email and that the transfer requests appeared consistent with his prior practice; the consumer fora rejected the bank's liability position but did not resolve criminal authorship.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Provider/login records and authenticated device/IP evidence linking the fraudulent email instructions to a specific operator and the destination accounts.
cases.disposition: NCDRC partly allowed the Bank's appeal only to remove the separate mental-agony compensation while confirming the substantive reimbursement order and other relief.
cases.case_summary: An NRI account holder told Canara Bank that his registered email had been hacked and asked that instructions from it not be acted upon. Months later, fraudulent transfer instructions associated with the compromised/imitated email identity were processed, and USD 86,500 was transferred from his NRE funds to banks abroad. State and national consumer proceedings examined the emails, bank statements, transfer requests and the bank's verification practices. They ultimately imposed liability on the bank, while leaving the criminal identity of the unknown email operator unresolved. The case adds a non-WhatsApp form of social engineering in which the directly manipulated humans were banking personnel rather than the account holder himself.
cases.research_notes: Primary source is the 2019 NCDRC appeal; the 2015 Kerala State Commission judgment is registered as a supporting T1 source. Amount uses the figure repeatedly stated in the adjudicatory record. Cross-border=yes reflects Doha context and overseas bank transfers.

actors.function_assignment_basis: Unknown operators issued transfer instructions while impersonating the account holder through a compromised/imitated email identity.
actors.conduct_assessed: Impersonating the NRE customer in email instructions to bank personnel.
actors.attribution_limitations: Consumer records do not resolve the sender, device, login origin or relationship to receiving accounts.
actors.relationship_note: Victim-facing function is toward bank employees who were induced to process instructions.

actors.function_assignment_basis: The adjudicatory record documents transfers to banks abroad but does not identify the controlling humans.
actors.conduct_assessed: Receiving/control of the overseas endpoints to which the NRE funds were transferred.
actors.attribution_limitations: Transfer destinations are documented, but public material reviewed does not resolve the humans controlling them.

cases.case_title: Fake Louis Philippe refund support and malicious-app fraud
cases.case_number: WA/364/2022; WP(C) No.1900/2022; Jalukbari P.S. Case No.1229/2021
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Louis Philippe customer-care manager handling a garment refund
cases.reconnaissance_description: The victim had recently purchased a Louis Philippe garment online and later received a brand-specific refund call. The brand subsequently reported a customer-database breach during the relevant period.
cases.initial_contact_summary: The victim received a phone call from a person posing as Louis Philippe customer care after seeking to return an online garment purchase.
cases.pretext_summary: The caller offered to process a INR 4,000 refund and instructed the victim to download a mobile application.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Brand-specific knowledge and refund context created legitimacy; later records noted a customer-data breach at the retailer.
cases.requested_action: Download a mobile application to receive a refund.
cases.victim_action: The victim downloaded the application; three unauthorized transactions totalling INR 94,204 followed.
cases.other_evidence: Bank transaction records, beneficiary-account records, OTP logs, complaint records and retailer email acknowledging a customer-database breach.
cases.attribution_target: Papendra Kumar's caller/beneficiary role and downstream transfer recipients.
cases.attribution_limitations: The appellate consumer/writ record identifies Papendra Kumar as the fraudster/respondent and documents a beneficiary account in his name, but it is not a criminal conviction and does not independently establish every technical step performed through the downloaded application.
cases.alternative_explanation: The proceeding centered on bank/customer liability, not a criminal trial of the identified respondent.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Device/application forensic evidence showing what the downloaded app did and directly tying the caller's device/account activity to the unauthorized transactions.
cases.disposition: Gauhati High Court dismissed SBI's writ appeal and upheld the direction to credit the unauthorized-transaction amount to the customer.
cases.case_summary: A Guwahati customer who wanted to return a Louis Philippe garment received a refund call from a person posing as the brand's customer-care manager. The caller instructed him to download a mobile app to receive INR 4,000. Three unauthorized transactions totalling INR 94,204 followed. The record identified Papendra Kumar as the caller/respondent, traced a substantial transfer to an account in his name and documented later movement of funds. The retailer also acknowledged a customer-database breach during the relevant period. The High Court treated the transactions as unauthorized and upheld relief against SBI. The case combines pretext-specific targeting, device compromise and a comparatively unusual overlap between a human-resolved victim-facing actor and a financial endpoint.
cases.research_notes: Identity resolution does not imply criminal guilt. The High Court proceeding adjudicated banking liability rather than criminal responsibility.

actors.attribution_limitations: The proceeding adjudicated bank/customer liability rather than criminal guilt and does not independently prove every technical action through the app.
actors.alternative_explanation: Criminal responsibility was not the issue finally determined in the writ appeal.
actors.relationship_note: Unusual case where a source resolves both victim-facing and financial functions to the same named human.

actors.conduct_assessed: Receiving onward transfers after the initial unauthorized transaction.
actors.attribution_limitations: The appellate record does not resolve the identities or knowledge of all downstream recipients.
